title: Thomas More and Erasmus
hook: two friends, a book called Utopia, and humor with holiness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Juan Diego, carrying flowers in his cloak to a bishop who doubted him. Your line was the little one. What did you do that felt too big for you? Day eight hundred forty-one.

A scholar is riding on horseback, the long way back from Italy to England, with hours to fill. Rather than waste them, he starts composing a joke in his head: a whole book spoken by Folly herself, a lady who praises fools and mocks the wise. He's on his way to stay with a friend in London, and the friend's name gives him the title. The scholar is Erasmus. The friend is Thomas More. Today's word is the two of them together.
screen: `A LONG RIDE FROM ITALY.` → `A BOOK SPOKEN BY FOLLY.` → `A FRIEND IN LONDON.`

segments.voice: Start with the pun. Erasmus wrote his book in Latin and gave it a Greek title, Moriae Encomium, the Praise of Folly. In his letter to More at the front of it, he explains: moria is the Greek word for folly, and it sounds like More's name. Then he adds that his friend is as far from folly as his name is close to it. A joke between friends, printed in a book. Next, the friend. Erasmus once wrote a long letter describing More for someone who had never met him. He paints a man whose face leans toward cheerfulness, who loved a good joke from boyhood, who could find something to enjoy in almost anyone, and who was at the same time serious about prayer and generous to the poor. Then, More's own book, Utopia. It describes an island where a traveler claims everything is run differently: property shared, gold despised, worship tolerant. The name is a made-up word, and the book itself plays games with it. Readers still argue about how much of it More meant and how much was a joke with a sting in it. That uncertainty is part of the fun. Finally, why it matters for holiness. More is a canonized saint. The stories told about his last days say he kept joking to the end. Wit, for him, didn't compete with faith. In the Douay-Rheims, Ecclesiastes says there is "A time to weep, and a time to laugh." These two friends seem to have taken both halves of that line seriously.
screen: `MORIA, AND MORE.` · `A FACE THAT LEANS TOWARD CHEER.` · `AN ISLAND CALLED UTOPIA.` · `A SAINT WHO KEPT JOKING.` · then, large: `A TIME TO LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember laughing with a friend. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one friend you've laughed with until you couldn't stop. Find the moment: where you were, what set it off, their face. Let a smile come if it wants to. If you pray, you can give thanks for that friend, by name. If you don't, just stay with the memory and let it warm the room. Then, after the bell, if you can, send that friend one line that might make them laugh. The bell holds the time.
Utopia. Thomas More's book about an island run differently, written while trading jokes in Latin with his friend Erasmus. Today's word.
Your line: witty and holy. Today, make one person laugh on purpose, kindly, and notice whether it cost your seriousness anything. Day eight hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Thomas More, with Saint John Fisher, on a shared feast in June; he is the patron of statesmen and politicians, and some lawyers' guilds take his name.

notes: Praise of Folly's dedicatory letter: composed on horseback while returning from Italy, the pun Moria/More, 'as far from folly as his name is close to it'. Paraphrased; confirm. The hook places the ride 'over the Alps, on his way to England' and the stay in More's London house; confirm.
Erasmus's letter to Ulrich von Hutten (1519): More's cheerful face, love of jokes from boyhood, devotion and generosity. Paraphrased; confirm.
Utopia: shared property, contempt for gold, religious toleration; the name's Greek wordplay is mentioned without giving an etymology. Confirm.
'The stories told about his last days say he kept joking to the end' (Roper's Life; the scaffold remark): attributed, not quoted.
Original: μωρία (folly); confirm accent and pronunciation.
howItsDone: shared feast of Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, June 22; More named patron of statesmen and politicians by John Paul II. Dates omitted.
Editor: the dedicatory letter says he composed the book riding back from Italy; 'over the Alps' is not in it, so hook, screen and fork now say 'from Italy'.
